title: MIPS Instructions, Registers and Operands
subtitle: Now the course gets practical: write real MIPS.

references.title: Instructions: Language of the Computer
references.topics: Operations of the computer hardware; operands (registers, memory, immediates); signed and unsigned numbers; logical operations; MIPS floating-point instructions

objectives: Name the MIPS registers and explain what the register file is
Use register, memory and immediate operands
Move data between memory and registers with lw and sw
Describe floating-point operands and the floating-point registers

steps.question: A single line, `add $s0, $s1, $s2`, is a complete instruction. Why does it name numbered places instead of variables like `total`?
clues: The hardware has no variable names, only numbered storage places.
MIPS gives every program 32 very fast places called **registers**.
Almost everything a program computes passes through them.

notes.explain: Let students try to say what a CPU would need to find a variable named `total`. The answer: a number, not a name.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: The register file

head: Name
Number
Typical use
rows: Return address of a procedure call

steps.why: Each register holds 32 bits. Operations run at register speed, so good programs keep their busy values here.
steps.real: A compiler decides which variables live in registers. Your C or Java loop counter is almost always in a register while the loop runs.

mistake.wrong: Register $zero can be changed like any other register.
mistake.right: $zero always reads 0. A write to it is ignored.

explainAgain.beginner: Registers are the numbered slots on the CPU's desk. The names ($t0, $s1) are just friendly labels for the numbers 8, 17 and so on.

notes.explain: Reveal row by row. Stress that the names are conventions the assembler understands; the hardware only sees the number.

steps.title: The register file as hardware

items: 32 registers of 32 bits each: 1,024 bits (128 bytes) in total
Two registers can be **read** and one **written** in the same clock cycle
Register $zero is wired to the value 0

steps.why: This is exactly why MIPS instructions name at most three registers, which you will see when we encode them (Class 7).

deeper.text: In the datapath (Class 10) the register file has two read ports and one write port, controlled by a RegWrite signal.

steps.question: Which register always holds the value 0?
steps.why: $zero is hard-wired to 0.
feedback: $t0 is a temporary you can change.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each register group with its usual job.
steps.why: Conventions let separately written procedures work together.

steps.title: Run it: try to change $zero

blocks.title: Try to change $zero
blocks.hint: Run it, then edit the program and try writing other registers.

steps.why: The hardware ignores writes to $zero, so it can serve as a free constant 0.

steps.question: Before you run it: after `addi $zero, $zero, 5` what will `$zero` hold?
steps.result: Writes to $zero are discarded, which is what lets MIPS use it as a free constant 0.

questions.a: A small, fast set of 32 registers inside the CPU that instructions read and write.

questions.q: How many bits name one MIPS register?

steps.title: Three kinds of operand

nodes.label: Register
nodes.note: The value is already in a register: fastest.

nodes.label: Immediate
nodes.note: The 16-bit constant is part of the instruction word.

nodes.label: Memory
nodes.note: Reached only by loads and stores, using a base register and an offset.

steps.why: The operand kind decides speed, instruction size and what the hardware must do.
steps.real: Adding 1 to a loop counter uses an immediate. Reading an array element uses memory. Everything between uses registers.

explainAgain.beginner: Registers are in your hands, immediates are written on the instruction itself, memory is a shelf across the room.

steps.title: Immediate operands

items: An immediate is a **16-bit signed** constant inside the instruction
It is sign-extended to 32 bits before use
Bigger constants need two instructions: `lui` (upper 16 bits) then `ori` (lower 16 bits)

steps.why: This follows the design principle "make the common case fast": most constants in programs are small.

steps.title: Try it: immediate range

blocks.title: How many values fit in an n-bit signed immediate?

stages.label: Split
stages.text: Half are negative, half are not

steps.why: MIPS uses n = 16, giving −32,768 to 32,767.

steps.question: The immediate field of `addi` is 16 bits and signed. Which constant does NOT fit?

reveal.text: 40,000 is larger than 32,767, so `addi` cannot hold it. The assembler uses `lui` + `ori` instead.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about operands is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. A register operand is read from the register file.
2. An immediate operand is stored inside the instruction.
3. Arithmetic instructions in MIPS can read operands directly from memory.
4. Memory operands are reached with lw and sw.
steps.explain: In MIPS, arithmetic works on registers and immediates only. Memory is reached by lw and sw (a load/store architecture).
steps.fix: Arithmetic instructions use registers only; lw and sw access memory.

steps.question: How many bits does the immediate field of `addi` have?
steps.why: The I-format has a 16-bit immediate field.
feedback: 26 bits is the J-format target field.
The whole instruction is 32 bits, so the immediate cannot take all of them.

steps.title: Arithmetic instructions

head: Instruction
Meaning
Example
rows: Same, but never trap on overflow

steps.why: Every arithmetic instruction names exactly three operands. That regularity keeps the hardware simple.
steps.real: A compiler turns an expression with four variables into several of these three-operand instructions.

mistake.wrong: One `add` instruction can add three numbers.
mistake.right: `add` has exactly two sources. Adding three numbers takes two instructions.

explainAgain.beginner: Think of a calculator that only has a two-number plus key. For three numbers you press it twice and keep the middle result in a temporary.

steps.question: g = 10, h = 20 are in $s1 and $s2; i = 3, j = 4 are in $s3 and $s4. After the program for `f = (g + h) - (i + j)`, what does $s0 (f) hold?
steps.result: Two temporaries hold the partial sums; sub combines them.

steps.title: Run it: f = (g + h) - (i + j)

blocks.title: Translated expression
blocks.program:
li $s1, 10
li $s2, 20
li $s3, 3
li $s4, 4
add $t0, $s1, $s2
add $t1, $s3, $s4
sub $s0, $t0, $t1
blocks.hint: Step through it. Edit the numbers to try your own.

steps.why: Temporaries ($t0, $t1) hold the two partial results.

steps.title: Logical instructions

head: Instruction
Operation
Example
rows: Shift left / right by a constant

steps.why: Shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ, and masking picks out single fields of a word.
steps.real: Graphics, networking and compression code is full of shifts and masks.

deeper.text: `nor` with $zero gives NOT: `nor $t0, $s1, $zero` flips every bit of $s1.

steps.title: Run it: bits and shifts

blocks.title: Logical instructions on 12 (1100) and 10 (1010)
blocks.program:
li $s1, 12
li $s2, 10
and $t0, $s1, $s2
or $t1, $s1, $s2
xor $t2, $s1, $s2
sll $t3, $s1, 2
srl $t4, $s1, 2

steps.why: Compare the results with the binary patterns: AND keeps common 1s, OR keeps any 1.

steps.question: If $s1 = 5, what does `sll $t0, $s1, 3` put in $t0?
steps.why: Shifting left by 3 multiplies by 8: 5 × 8 = 40.
feedback: Shift is not the same as add.

steps.statement: `addu` and `add` give different results when the sum fits in 32 bits.
steps.why: They differ only on overflow: `add` traps, `addu` wraps.

steps.title: Loads and stores
steps.why: Only loads and stores touch memory, so every memory operand needs an explicit instruction.
steps.real: Reading an array element in C is a lw; writing one is a sw.

mistake.wrong: `lw $t0, 6($s1)` is fine if $s1 is a multiple of 4.
mistake.right: A word address must be a multiple of 4. Offset 6 breaks that, so the load is misaligned.

notes.explain: Memory is byte-addressed; a word is four bytes, so array element i of words is at base + 4 × i. Class 6 goes deeper.

steps.title: Run it: A[2] = A[0] + A[1]

blocks.title: Array in memory
blocks.hint: $s1 holds the base address 0x10010000 of the array A.

steps.why: Offsets are in bytes: element 1 is at +4, element 2 at +8.

steps.question: `$s3` holds the base address of array A (words). What byte offset does `A[3]` have?

reveal.text: Each word is 4 bytes, so A[3] is at offset **3 × 4 = 12**.

steps.result: Index × 4 gives the byte offset for an array of words.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put the instructions for A[1] = A[0] + 5 in order.
items: Load A[0] from memory into a register
steps.why: The value must be loaded before it is changed, and stored afterward.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about memory is wrong. Click it.
lines: 2. A word occupies four consecutive bytes.
3. `lw $t0, 6($s1)` is always fine when $s1 is a multiple of 4.
steps.explain: 6 is not a multiple of 4, so the address is misaligned and the load faults.
steps.fix: Use an offset that keeps the address a multiple of 4.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why does MIPS have separate lw and sw instructions instead of letting `add` read memory directly?
steps.answer: Memory is slow and varies in speed. Keeping arithmetic on registers makes every arithmetic instruction the same simple length and speed, which is easy to build and to speed up. Loads and stores handle the slow part separately.

notes.explain: Link back to Class 4: load/store architecture.

steps.title: Constants and register moves

items: Large constants become `lui` + `ori`, so one `li` can be **two** machine instructions
Pseudo-instructions are conveniences the assembler expands

steps.why: You write friendly code and the assembler turns it into real instructions.

steps.title: Run it: a large constant

blocks.title: li with a constant too big for 16 bits
blocks.hint: Step twice and watch the two real instructions.

steps.why: 100,000 = 0x186A0: upper half 1, lower half 0x86A0.

steps.question: How many real instructions does `li $t0, 70000` become?
steps.why: 70,000 does not fit in 16 bits, so `lui` and `ori` are used: 2 instructions.
feedback: That works only for constants from −32,768 to 65,535.
Two are enough: set the upper half, then OR in the lower half.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Why does MIPS have only 32 registers instead of thousands?
ideas: A register number must fit in 5 bits inside every instruction.
A bigger register file is slower to read (smaller is faster).
Most programs keep only a few values busy at once.
More registers mean more state to save on every procedure call.

steps.title: Floating-point operands

items: A double uses an even/odd **pair**, for example `$f0`

steps.why: Floating-point numbers have their own formats and hardware, so they get their own registers and instructions (the formats come in Class 9).
steps.real: Science, graphics and machine-learning code runs mostly on floating-point instructions.

mistake.wrong: Use `add` on $f registers to add floats.
mistake.right: Floating-point values need `add.s` or `add.d`; `add` works on integer registers.

notes.explain: The simulator in this course does not run floating point; treat these as notation to recognize.

steps.question: Which instruction adds two double-precision numbers?
steps.why: The suffix .d means double precision.
feedback: `addu` is the integer add without overflow trap.

steps.statement: The registers $f0 - $f31 are the same registers as $s0 - $s7.
steps.why: They are a separate register file for floating-point values.

steps.question: Name the register that always holds 0, the register for a return address, and the registers used for temporaries.
steps.solution: $zero is wired to 0, $ra holds the return address of a procedure call, and $t registers are temporaries.

steps.question: Variables f, g, h, i are in $s0, $s1, $s2, $s3. Write MIPS for f = g + h - i.
steps.solution: Add g and h into a temporary, then subtract i and put the result in f ($s0). Each instruction has exactly three operands.
steps.mistake: Trying to write one instruction with four operands.

steps.question: The base address of array A (words) is in $s3. Translate A[5] = A[3] + 7.
steps.solution: A[3] is at offset 3 × 4 = 12 and A[5] at 5 × 4 = 20. Load, add the immediate 7, store back.
steps.mistake: Using the index as the offset (3 and 5) instead of index × 4.

steps.question: A redesigned ISA uses 12-bit signed immediates. What range of constants fits in one instruction?
steps.solution: 12 bits give 2^12 = 4,096 values; half are negative: −2^11 = −2,048 to 2^11 − 1 = 2,047.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: Variables g and h are in $s1 and $s2; the base of array A is in $s3. Write MIPS for g = h + A[8].
steps.solution: A[8] is at byte offset 8 × 4 = 32. Load it into $t0, then add h.
steps.title: Exam practice: translation

steps.question: Trace the program and give the final values of $s2 and $s3.
steps.solution: $s1 = 6; sll by 3 multiplies by 8, so $s2 = 48; sub gives $s3 = 48 − 6 = 42.
steps.title: Exam practice: trace

steps.question: Explain why MIPS arithmetic instructions use only registers and immediates, never memory.
steps.answer: Registers are fast and need only 5 bits to name, so instructions stay simple and the same length. Memory access is separated into lw and sw (a load/store design), which keeps each instruction regular and easy to speed up.
steps.solution: A good answer links register speed, the small number of bits needed, and the load/store separation to simpler hardware.
steps.mistake: Saying memory is not used at all: it is used, but only through loads and stores.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: MIPS has 32 registers of 32 bits; a register number takes 5 bits.
$zero is always 0; $t are temporaries, $s are saved, $a pass arguments, $v return values, $ra holds the return address.
Operands are registers, 16-bit immediates, or memory (reached only by lw and sw).
Arithmetic instructions name exactly three operands.
An array element i of words is at base + 4 × i bytes.
Large constants need lui + ori; floating point has its own registers and instructions.

mistakes.wrong: Arithmetic instructions can read memory directly.
mistakes.right: Only lw and sw access memory.

mistakes.wrong: Array index equals the byte offset.
mistakes.right: The byte offset is index × 4 for words.

mistakes.wrong: Floating-point values use the integer registers.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: MIPS has 32 registers; instructions work on registers and immediates and reach memory only through lw and sw. Arithmetic and logical instructions always name three operands. Arrays are addressed as base plus four times the index, constants beyond 16 bits take lui and ori, and floating point has separate registers and instructions.

questions.question: In `addi $t0, $s1, 25`, what kind of operand is 25?
questions.why: It is a constant stored in the instruction.
questions.misconception: A register would be written with a $ sign.

questions.question: How many bits are needed to name one MIPS register?
questions.misconception: The number of names is 2 to the number of bits.

questions.question: With $s1 = 9, $s2 = 4, $s3 = 2, $s4 = 1, what does $s0 hold after `add $t0,$s1,$s2` / `add $t1,$s3,$s4` / `sub $s0,$t0,$t1`?
questions.misconception: Add each pair first, then subtract.

questions.question: If $s1 = 5, what is $t0 after `sll $t0, $s1, 3`?
questions.misconception: A left shift by n multiplies by 2 to the n.

questions.question: Which sequence performs A[4] = A[1] + 3 (base in $s3)?
questions.why: A[1] is at offset 4 and A[4] at offset 16.
questions.misconception: Byte offsets are index × 4; also read first, then store.

questions.question: $s1 = 0x1002. What happens when `lw $t0, 0($s1)` executes?
options: An alignment fault: 0x1002 is not a multiple of 4
questions.why: A word load needs an address that is a multiple of 4.

questions.question: `li $t0, 70000` is expanded by the assembler. What does the first real instruction load into the upper 16 bits?
questions.why: 70,000 = 0x11170: the upper 16 bits are 1 (lui), and ori adds 0x1170.
questions.misconception: 70,000 divided by 65,536 gives 1 with a remainder.

items.q: How many registers does MIPS have and how many bits name one?
Name the three kinds of operand.
What is the offset of A[i] for an array of words?
items.a: 4 × i bytes from the base address.
